- Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. The Ottawa Citizen in this morning's issue publishes the letter of resignation of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peek) from the Committee of Pensions and Reestablishment. In that letter the following statements are made:	.
I therefore resign, not only to protest in the naipe of the widows of the hundreds of brave men whom I had the honour of leading in the late war, but as a protest against a deplorable attempt on two successive days to camouflage the incident, and also as a protest in the name of common honesty and decency. With the consent of the Pensions Committee, I desire to state that at this morning's session, on the written request of Mr. C. S. McLean), the whole question was fully investigated and the original stenographic notes-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. member rises to a question of privilege on behalf of the committee, or on behalf of himself? In either case, I have to point out that it is a well-established rule of the House that there can be no reference in the House to the proceedings of any committee of the House until the report of that committee is before the House for consideration. Bearing that in mind, it is somewhat difficult to know how the hon. gentleman could properly refer to the proceedings before a committee, that committee not having reported.

The question of privilege is one in which I as chairman of the committee, am distinctly involved. I make this explanation on my own behalf, although I make it with the consent of the committee.
The whole question was fully investigated and the original stenographic notes were transcribed under oath by Mr. Blue.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret very much to have to interrupt the hon. member, but if he desires to take exception to some statement with reference to himself which has been made in the public press, and to give a denial thereto, he -would be in order on a question of privilege. On the other hand, if he wishes -to set right a proceeding which took place before a committee of the House he certainly would not be in order in doing so at this stage.
I would ask the unanimous consent of the House to put this statement on record.

In view of the position which this matter has assumed, both for members of Parliament and the public, it seems to me it would be well that an explanation of it should be heard, and I hope that the unanimous consent of the House will be given.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course, the House can give its unanimous consent, and under the circumstances I have very great pleasure in putting the question whether the hon. member shall have the unanimous consent of the House to make his statement.

If it be in accordance with the rules might I ask the hon. gentleman who leads the Government to repeat the remarks he has just made. I did not hear a syllable of them, and therefore I could not possibly act intelligently on a question based on any argument he delivered to the House.

What I intended to say was this: Inasmuch as this matter has assumed a good deal of prominence and is of interest both to members of Parliament and to the public outside, I think it would be well that an authoritative statement should be made and go out to the country, and in that sense I think it would be a wise proceeding for us to give unani

mous consent to hearing a statement from the responsible chairman of the committee.

Is the hon.
member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) present:

If the hon. member is allowed to make a statement by unanimous consent, I should like to know how far the House will be allowed to go into the whole question. I should like to know exactly how far we are going against what is the rule, as stated by yourself, Mr. Speaker.

Where we would seem to get would be this: Instead of having conflicting statements first from one side and then from the other, we should have what I suppose might be considered a disinterested authoritative statement from the chairman of the committee.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There can be no debate upon the calling of the Orders of the. Day. I take it that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) does not give his consent to the statement being made by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn).

I do not want to put myself in opposition to any sentiment that is general all over the House, but I should like to know on what ground the leader of the House can call the statement of the chairman of the committee the authoritative statement. speechtext: The House resumed, from May 5, consideration in committee of Bill No. 12 (Hon. Mr. Guthrie) respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise.-Mr. Boivin in -the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When progress was last reported upon this Bill all of the clauses and -schedules had been read and considered. Paragraph (k) of clause 2, clauses, 29, 32, 37, 44, 45, 63 and 101, the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Gloucester to clause 37 and by the hon. the Acting Solicitor 'General to clauses .29. 44 and 101 have -been allowed to stand for further consideration. The other clauses have been adopted. Clauses 19 and 76 which provide for the expenditure of money cannot be adopted until the House has concurred in the required resolution. The question is upon the amendment proposed to clause 29. Shall the amendment carry?
What is the amendment, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Guthrie moves to amend clause 29 by adding to the said clause the following words: .
Provided that no disability imposed by paragraph (b) of subsection 4 of section S of " The Naturalization Act," chapter thirty-eight of the Statutes of 1919, (first session) shall disentitle a person on that ground alone to the said certificate.

Last night wdien we had a discussion on this clause the Acting Solicitor 1 General intimated that it was not the intention of the Act to disfranchise any one, but when my hon. friend from Lambton urged that those who had been in this country for a certain number of years and had proved them-selves good citizens should be afforded some means whereby to acquire citizenship in order to enable them to vote at elections, the Naturalization Act was raised as the bar sinister to any such proposition. I gathered from the remarks that were made in that respect that the Naturalization Act was regarded by a great many hon. gentlemen on the other side as something sacred. British citizenship, in the minds of those hon. .gentlemen, is a holy ark that ought to be surrounded by every safeghard and precaution so that its purity
may remain absolutely inviolate. Now, Mr. Chairman, accepting that high moral creed of my hon. friends, I do not see why, when the Naturalization Act says that the wife of a British subject is a British subject and the wife of an alien is an alien, we should give *0 male British subjects the right to vote but deny their wives, who happen to be alien, the privilege their husbands enjoy. We cannot contend that these women have been remiss in the duties of citizenship because they 'have not personally claimed naturalization. By law they have the same status as their husbands in regard to citizenship. But to-day we are say-mg to them that unless they were born on the American continent they must go to a judge and get him to certify that they are entitled to vote, in spite of the fact that the law says they can. Among those voters wlw are naturalized by law there are many Italians and Belgians who are married to French women: and the conclusion has forced itself upon me that the Government is introducing the Naturalization Act in this case because they are afraid of the votes of these women. They know that the women are more sensitive to injustice than perhaps men are, and they are afraid that the uses and abuses to which Orders in Council have been put, and the nefarious ways in which the business of the country has been conducted, will be keenly felt by the women. If this ark of British citizenship is so profoundly sacred to my hon. friends opposite, why in reason's name should they desecrate in order to deprive certain inoffensive and innocent people from a right which belongs to them? If the 'Government are afraid of the female vote let them be manly enough to come out and say so and eliminate entirely the enfranchisement of the other sex. If they are afraid that the women will go against them let them say outright that no women shall have the vote. But if the women deserve full citizenship by way of recognition of all that they have done in behalf of the country and the intelligence they have shown, then I say that they ought to be put on the same footing as men. I for one cannot support a measure that will tend to make the franchise more difficult for women who are entitled to it than for men, merely by reason of their sex.

Clause 29 which gives the qualification of electors reads: 1
(1)	Save as in this Act otherwise provided, every person, male or female, shall be qualified to^ vote at the election of a member who, not being: an Indian ordinarily resident on an 133
Indian reservation,
(a)	is a British subject by birth or naturalization ; and,
(b)	is of the full age of twenty-one years-and,
(c)	has ordinarily resided in Canada for at least twelve months and in the electoral district wherein such person seeks to vote for at least two months immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election.
If I understand the first paragraph correctly, every man and every woman in *Canada who is a British subject, twenty-one years of age, and has resided in the electoral district for at least twelve months prior to the election, will be given a vote. This first paragraph establishes a very broad basis for the electoral franchise. When the minister introduced the Bill about a month ago he said that he and the Government generally wanted a fair, broad and generous franchise. His wishes would have been more completely carried out if paragraph 2 had been omitted andi the section confined to the first paragraph. Paragraph 2 is as follows:
For the purposes of this Act, the allegiance or nationality of a person, as it was at the birth of such person, shall be deemed incapable of being changed, or of having, been changed, merely by reason or in consequence of marriage or -change of allegiance or naturalization of any other person, or otherwise than by personal naturalization of such first mentioned person. Provided, however, -that this subsection shall not apply to any person born on -the continent of North America, nor to any person who in person applies -to and obtains from any judge having jurisdiction in naturalization proceedings, a -certificate under -the hand of such judge and the seal, if any, of his court, to the effect following:
Then follows the certificate. As I understand it, this second paragraph limits and- -restricts the basis upon which the franchise is granted in the first part of the section, having the effect of excluding the wives and children of naturalized British subjects in Canada-wives and children who have not personally -been naturalized, but -who are British subjects on account of the naturalization of husband or father.
When this clause -first came up for discussion before the committee, the member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) pointed out that its effect would be to disfranchise a considerable number of persons; that if the -electoral law was read in conjunction with the Naturalization Act, persons who were not at present naturalized would have to wait ten years before -they could obtain their certificate of naturalization, and would therefore be unable to obtain the franchise until 1928. The Acting Solicitor General



yesterday brought in the following amendment to section 29:
Provided that no disability imposed by paragraph Ob) of subsection 4 of section 8 of "The Naturalization Act," chapter 38 of the statutes of 1519 (first session), shall disentitle a person on that ground alone to the said certificate.
That amendment has reference to the following subsection in the Naturalization Act:
No certificate of naturalization shall, before the expiration of a period of ten years after the termination of the present war, be granted in Canada to any subject of a country which at the time of the passing of this Act was at war with His Majesty, but this provision shall not apply to a person who,
(1)	having served in His Majesty's forces or in the forces of His Majesty's Allies or of any country acting in naval or military co-operation with His Majesty was not discharged from such service by reason of his enemy nationality, sympathy or associations; or,
(2)	is a member of a race or community known to be opposed to the enemy governments ; or,
(3)	was at birth a British subject.
As I understand it, the Acting Solicitor General's amendment relates not to the case of women and children, but simply to the case of the men. But the men are in no way affected by section 29, so that the amendment does not in any way improve that section. The amendment provides that even though certain persons may not be naturalized for ten years to come, they are not debarred from obtaining a certificate. Women and children do not need to be naturalized, Mr. Chairman. Section 11 of the Naturalization Act provides that the wife of a British subject shall be deemed to be a British subject-not by birth, not by naturalization; simply a British subject.
Take the case of an American who came to Canada and was naturalized and became a British subject after having lived in Canada the necessary length of time; the wife of that American becomes a British subject by the mere fact that her husband has become a British subject. An Austrian crossed over to America, came to Canada and was naturalized and became a British subject under our law. In accordance with the provisions of the Naturalization Act, the wife of that Austrian is a British subject. It cannot be denied-and the statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) last night bears me out-that the wife of a British subject by naturalization or by birth is a British subject no matter whether her husband is an Austrian, a German, an American, a Frenchman, or a Belgian.
IMr. Cannon.1
Now, what about the children? Section 13 of the Naturalization Act, subsection 1, provides that the children of a man who is a naturalized British subject are themselves British subjects unless the father chooses subsequently to change his own nationality. Therefore I say that according to the Act as it reads now, the wife and the children of a British subject by naturalization are British subjects. The argument brought forward yesterday by the Acting Solicitor General, by the President of the Privy Council, and even by the Minister of Justice, was to the effect that section 29 had to be put in the law on account of the Naturalization Act as it now reads, and that it would be impossible for this Parliament to amend, change or alter that Act because it was the result of an agreement between the Canadian Government and the Imperial Government. I say, Mr. Chairman, that this is no argument at all, because even if the Naturalization Act remains as it is to-day, these women and children are British subjects, and should and would be given a vote under our Franchise Act if paragraph two of section 29 was not added to the law.
As to the amendment which is proposed by the Acting Solicitor General I think it has no bearing on the case. Section two is an amendment to the Naturalization Act. The ministers and the supporters of the Government have contended that we should not touch the Naturalization Act- that if we did so it would be a breach of faith with the Imperial authorities. Well, what did the Government do? They introduced a paragraph in clause 29 of this Franchise Act which in itself is ,an amendment to the Naturalization Act, because it expressly says that people who are British subjects according to the existing law will not be treated as British subjects at election time but will have to follow special methods and follow a special piocess before they are given a ballot. It says, Mr. Chairman, that a woman -who, according to section eleven, is a British subject in every way, shape or form, will have to go before a tribunal, and will have to be given a certificate, and that a judge who refuses to give that certificate will have the right to debar that person who is a British subject by law from casting her vote at an election. Paragraph two has also the same result and. the same consequence as regards the children. According to the Naturalization Act these children are British subjects. The first paragraph of clause 29 of the franchise law says that all Brit-

ish subjects aged twenty-one years, and having a certain period of residence in Canada, are entitled to vote. Notwithstanding the fact that these children may have lived in Canada for thirty years and, that they are British subjects for all other purposes, despite the fact that they are British citizens cannot be denied or challenged, the Government introduced into this law a subparagraph to clause 29 which means that those children will have to go before a judge or a tribunal and will have to' obtain a certificate before they are placed on the same level or the same standing as every other British subject in this country. I say, Mr. Chairman, that this is altogether unfair and altogether arbitrary, and that this subparagraph ought to be struck out of the Bill altogether. The Minister of the Interior, speaking in the name of and on behalf of the Government, rose in this House the other day and said that the remarks made by the member for Waterloo (Mr. Euler) " have shown that there is such a condition and such a state of things in Canada that we ought to bring in. an amendment." The amendment was brought in, but I ask the Minister of the Interior-or any other member of the Government, or any supporter of the Government-to explain how the amendment brought in yesterday can help these wives or help these children to whom I have referred. The amendment simply refers to a clause saying that within ten years after the termination of war no naturalization certificate shall be issued. These women and children do not need these naturalization certificates. According to the law of the country they are British subjects; and the Government by this law is bimply withdrawing from them rights which were guaranteed to them-firstly when they were naturalized through the operation .of law; and secondly-rights which were guaranteed anew when the Naturalization Act of 1919 was passed by this Parliament.
I assert, that the present debate is one of the most important that ever took place in' this House. Are we, once and for all, going to lay down the rule that this country will malre a contract with people and respect that contract, or are we going to lay down the rule that we can bring people into this country under false pretenses, and break the contracts that we made with those people and the laws which protect them vThen it suits our purposes, and treat our existing law-our existing certificates of naturalization and the sovereign rights of citizenship 133*	-
in this country-as an ordinary scrap of paper? I think the Government has no right to do that, and that the House should exercise such a pressure upon it that the clause will be changed and every man, woman and child in Canada will know justice and fairness shall prevail when it comes to the rights of the franchise.
Mr. COWAN; When did we enter into a contract with the wives of aliens to whom the hon. gentleman has referred, that they would have the right to vote when they came into Canada?

The law of our country
says that if the hon. member for Regina comes from Belgium, settles in Regina, lives there for a certain period of years, and behaves himself in such a way as to show himself to be a good citizen, he is to be given a certificate of naturalization, and.he becomes a British subject, enjoying all the rights and privileges of British citizenship, and that his wife and children also have the same privileges and the same rights. That is the law.

We are only giving that
privilege to them now. Consequently we never had any previous contract with the parties to whom my hon. friend refers.

I am awfully sorry to disagree with the hon. member but I know something about the law of my country and the rule-which is just as old as the naturalization law itself-is to the effect that the naturalization of a British subject carries with it the naturalization of his wife. So much is this the case that I might quote to my hon. friend the old French saying which declares as regards the wife, "Qui prend mari prend pays," "She who takes a husband takes his country." Who ever heard, Mr. Chairman, that in any properly organized country the husband can be of one nationality, and that the wife in the same household should be of another nationality?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
You will find it in the
United States.
Mr. CANNON. Who ever heard that in any properly politically organized country the husband could he of one nationality, the wife of another nationality, and the children of a third nationality? Laws are based on rules of common sense. But what is the position created by this law? The Government, afraid of what they call the foreign vote, have taken, I may say, a circuitous means of excluding from the polls people

who are British subjects and who have a right to record their votes at the next election.
The other night I heard the member for Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) discussing this question. I have great, respect for that gentleman, but to tell the truth, Mr. Chairman, I have more respect for his opinions on railway matters than I have for his opinions on naturalization laws. The member for Algoma was basing his arguments on this question: Are we going to admit on an equal footing at the polls our enemies of yesterday. Then with his usual fluency the hon. member made a very patriotic appeal to this committee. But that is not the question at all, Mr. Chairman. We do not want to take our enemies of yesterday and put them on an equal footing with Canadian citizens we are onljr asking that those who are British subjects should remain so not only when it comes to making private contracts, not only when it comes to paying taxes, but that they should be British subjects even when it comes to exercising the franchise. That is what we want.
There is a principle of constitutional law, which is well recognized in every country living under the British constitution-the principle of no taxation without representation. We were told yesterday that people who died a hundred ye .rs ago should not be quoted in this House. I think that that ruling is very hard on our Lord who died two thousand years ago. But I will refer to the history of England, and that history records that the greatest constitutional struggles were fought to establish that principle of, no taxation without representation. To-day in this House we may be divided as Liberals on the one side and as Tories on the other, but the Tories of today were the Liberals of a hundred years ago. There are no such Tories either in Canada or outside as there were in England only a hundred or a hundred and fifty years ago.
They are a couple of generations behind.

I say that every public man ought to support the principle for which John Hampden fought, the principle which brought about the English Revolution, the principle which brought Charles the First to the scaffold-a principle which is not only radical and liberal, but which should be respected by every man who knows anything about the history of England or appreciates constitutional liberty. To-day the wives and children of these British subjects are treated as citizens of Can-

ada, and as such they have to pay their share of taxation into the public purse. They were British subjects yesterday, they are British subjects to-day, and they will be British subjects to-morrow notwithstanding the provisions of the franchise law, and I contend that we have no right to exclude them from the franchise.
I admire the way in which the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) has conducted this Bill through committee. He was always willing to accept every fair suggestion whether made by hon. members on his own side or by hon. members on this side of the House. And the question that I put to him to-day, through, you, Mr. Chairman, is one that should appeal to a member of the Bar and to a legal mind. I ask the Acting Solicitor General, through you, Mr. Chairman, to say: Is it a fair legal proposition to say, on the one hand, that a woman is a British subject, enjoying all the rights and privileges of British citizenship and, on the other hand, to say that, notwithstanding her British citizenship, she will not be allowed to vote, or will be allowed to vote only after having gone through certain formalities that no other British subject in Canada is obliged to go through? Is it fair, is it legal, is it logical? I say that it is not fair, and I think I have proved that it is not fair. I say that it is not legal, because the status of a person cannot be changed by one law and re-established by the other. To-day either I am a British subject or I am not; and if I am a British subject in the one sense, I am a British [DOT]subject in every other sense. Therefore not only is it not fair, and not legal, but it is not logical.
How can you expect these people to understand that Canada is a land of democracy and of freedom if you treat them in this way? How can you expect them to have faith in the future of our country if to-day, to suit the whim of a small faction on the Government side that represents the prejudices of a small section of the people of this country, these British subjects are turned away from the polls as if they were not worthy to cast their vote and help decide our political issues?
I do hope that the Acting Solicitor General will reconsider this clause and will see to it that every British subject in Canada be given a vote. When this Bill was introduced the Acting Solicitor General declared from his seat that the franchise was to be given to every British subject of the age of twenty-one years having the requisite qualifications as to residence. Here are British subjects-British subjects according

to the law passed in 1919, yet notwithstanding that law, notwithstanding the declaration of the Acting Solicitor General, these people will be deprived of their right to vote unless they have pre-4 p.m. viously obtained a certificate.
I have seen examples of the most intricate pieces of legislation introduced by this Government, but I assert that this particular legislation is without parallel, and I challenge any hon. member to cite similar legislation passed by any democratic country which claims to be guided by ideals of freedom and liberty. We are not asking-and I repeat it, Mr. Chairman-we are not asking that our enemies of yesterday be given the vote and be put on the same footing as British subjects but we are asking that justice be done to people who were British subjects yesterday, who are British subjects to-day, and who will be British subjects to-morrow. That is our whole case. It is a case of fairness, it is a case of justice, and it is a case that ought to be favourably considered by the Government. What remedy is proposed by the amendment drafted by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen)? None at all. The amendment has no bearing on section 29.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Just to clear that matter up-if there is any question about that, we are not going to press the amendment.
The point I wish to make is this. The Acting Solicitor General says in this House: "What we want is fairness." The hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Euler) gets up-	i

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I understood it was the hon. member for Waterloo North who wanted this.

I do not know who wanted it, but I will explain what I think of it. My hon. friend (Mr. Euler) makes certain declarations in this House. The Government, officially, through the mouth of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), says: "we shall see that that condition of things disappears and that a proper remedy is brought in." This is the remedy, and I defy any member of the Government to prove that the remedy, as drafted, and as introduced by the Acting Solicitor General, has any bearing whatsoever on clause 29 concerning women and children. There is another class, a class of people who are not British subjects, or who have lost their certificates of naturalization. The hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) said that those people who are not British
subjects, who never cared to be naturalized, although they may have lived for years in Canada, showed that they did not deserve to become British subjects. The hon. member may be right in certain cases, but this is not the case of all the persons referred to. At the time of Confederation in 1867- this is political history known to every member of the House-it was agreed between the two existing parties at that time that foreigners living in Ontario would be given the right to vote without their being sworn in any way. What was the result? Those people went to the polls; they were admitted as electors; they were granted, every right and privilege of British citizenship, and they naturally never thought oi going before a court or -a judge to obtain a certificate, as the Government of this country were giving them all the rights and privileges of British citizenship. Most ot those people are now dead; some, but only a few, still live. But what about their children, born outside of 'Canada, people who may be now forty, fifty, sixty years of age, who have lived in Canada practically all their lives? If their fathers were not British subjects, strictly speaking, according to the law, if those boys or girls were born outside of Canada, they are not British subjects. Could not something be done for those people, who are not foreigners who arrived in this country only two or three or five years ago, but who are people who have lived in Canada, for twenty-five, thirty or forty years and who are good citizens, in some cases the best citizens of this country?
Shall Canada refuse to do something for them? We are answered by the statement that the Imperial Act adopted by the Parliament of Canada cannot be amended. Let that be so; but why not add to clause 29 of this Bill a very simple paragraph stating that people who have lived in this country for ten or fifteen years, who had formerly been given the ballot, should have a right to vote, just as we did for the Indians last night, for the purposes of this Act? That would not be giving naturalization. We would not be putting aside the Naturalization Act of 1919; but we would be fair and just; we would be giving to those people something to which they are entitled. It was very simple for the Acting Solicitor General last night to amend the Indian Act as regards the franchise. He simply proposed the insertion of a clause whereby an Indian under certain conditions would have a right to vote. The Indian Act says expressly that no Indian has a right to vote in this country.

The amendment is good and I supported it; but if it be as easy as that for the Acting Solicitor General to go through the Indian Act-

with the Indian Act, as my hon. friend must see.

That is exactly the point I am making. By giving, under our electoral law, the right to vote to an Indian, although the Indian Act expressly says that an Indian, ordinarily resident on a reserve, being a ward of the Government, has no right to vote,-

Has not the Franchise Act always said that?
Mr. 'GUTHRIE: The franchise is not something that is born with us; it is something that is conferred. Heretofore we have not conferred it on the Indians; now we are conferring it on certain Indians,

hut there is no disqualification as regards the franchise in the Indian Act. The enfranchised Indian in the Indian Act,-I learned this only last night-is an Indian who has been given his liberty, not the vote. That is the sense in which the word is Used in the Indian Act.
The Acting Solicitor General is perfectly right-, but we are not discussing the same thing.

My point is this, that according to the existing law in Canada, an Indian, ordinarily living on an Indian Reserve, being a ward of the Government, has no right to vote at an election.
