speechtext: That is right.

We shall soon understand one another. The Acting Solicitor General says that that is the law. Therefore, an Indian living on an Indian Reserve, being a ward of the Government, who was a member o-f the Canadian army or the Imperial army, or an Allied army, has no vote according to the franchise law. (So, I say that the Naturalization Act says that unless a man is a naturalized or a born British subject, he has no right to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing in the Naturalization Act about voting.

I say that in the Naturalization Act a British subject is a man who is a British subject either by birth or by naturalization, and the Franchise Act says that only British subjects will have a right to vote under certain conditions. Why not put into our Franchise Act a clause covering a class of people who have lived in Canada for a certain number of years, who have, been peaceable, dutiful citizens of this country for, say twenty or twenty-five years, but who are not British subjects on account of circumstances that I have explained and that other hon. members have explained to the committee (better than myself? It is just as easy for this committee to insert this special clause as it was for the committee to adopt that special clause in connection with Indians. We shall not interfere with the Naturalization Act which will remain as it is now, but for the -purposes of the franchise, we shall have a special clause covering the case of those people. As regards clause 29, if the Acting Solicitor General wishes to give to this House a token of his fair-mindedness, which we all appreciate, he ought

to move first that >subclause 2 be struck out altogether, and second, that there be substituted for subclause 2 a clause covering the case of the people "whom I have just mentioned. He ought to move first that subsection 2 be struck out, and secondly, that in itis place there be inserted a paragraph covering the case of the people I have just mentioned.

My hon. friend (Mr. Cannon) has made a very elaborate argument upon entirely false premises. Speaking broadly, my hon. friend based his argument upon this principle, that the fact of being a Bi-itish subject absolutely entitles one to the franchise.
A British subject is entitled to the franchise if he has the necessary qualifications as to age and residence. That is the law.

The correction does not alter the point I am going to make. In support of his contention he proceeded to argue that the principle was based upon hundreds of years of practice under the British constitution, and he cited the revolutions at the time of King Charles and at other periods of British history, when certain vital principles respecting taxation and other matters were contended for by the people. Upon the principles which, as he alleged, were then at stake he bases his argument to-day for the enfranchisement of the particular class he refers to. He forgets, however, that the franchise as we have it to-day is a comparatively modern institution. Universal franchise was certainly unknown and most certainly was not accepted or practised at the time he refers to, when these great principles -were fought out. The universal franchise comes within the memory of most members of this House. It is a comparatively new proposition. Furthermore, if my hon. friend wishes to base his argument oh constitutional procedure he should remember that the franchise has been extended from time to time by Act of Parliament. The franchise is a gift; it is something that is granted to the subject. I would also point out that while the fact of being a British subject certainly entitles an individual to the protection of the laws of a country it does not necessarily follow that it entitles him to vote. I carry my hon. friend a step further, and he will correct me if I quote him wrongly. He suggests that we should incorporate in this Bill a clause that if a person has been resident in this country ten or fifteen years, whether he is a British subject under the
Naturalization Act or not, he should be entitled to vote. That is an extraordinary doctrine, and I know of no precedent for it in British constitutional history.

I made two different propositions. First, as regards the wives and children. I said that as British subjects they should be given the franchise. Secondly, as regards the men who have lived here in Canada for quite a number of years, but who for certain reasons are not British subjects, I said there should be a clause to cover these special cases, giving them the right to vote.

Can this House imagine a more extraordinary proposal than that an individual, simply because he has been resident in the country and obeying the laws of the country for a certain length of time, should be entitled to the vote, although he is not a natural-born or naturalized British subject? I have never heard of such a doctrine, and certainly no democratic or autocratic country either on the face of the globe ever heard such a proposal made , seriously in its legislative assembly.
Let us look at this particular class. I think my hon. friend has beclouded the issue entirely. The point we are discussing is whether or not we shall extend the franchise to the wives of men who came to us from foreign countries, the men having been resident in Canada. Under the old laws of citizenship a woman from Austria, for instance, could come here and if on the day she landed, she got married to a British subject, by law she became a British subject that very day. I am taking an extreme case perhaps, but it is only by taking such a case that we can appreciate the point my hon. friend is trying to make. His proposal is that women, when naturalized by law, should at once be entitled to vote. I submit that that would be a preposterous proposition. Let us take a case that is not so extreme or so specific. By the progress of events and by recent legislation the franchise has been generally extended to women in this country. That is looked upon as the most progressive step in enfranchisement that we have taken in the past five years. Now what are we doing here? We are simply saying that the women aliens who came to our country and who married British subjects should show that they have the qualifications which their husbands must have in order to be naturalized. It seems to me that is a common sense proposition. More than that, if we

were not to exercise some care in extending the franchise, I believe we would be derelict in our duty to the country at large. We must be very careful to see that the ' franchise is exercised only by those who have an intelligent understanding of the affairs of the country. I think in the past we have been altogether too careless in naturalizing people. We- have naturalized persons who did not understand either of the two languages spoken in this country, and who had no knowledge of our democratic principles and institutions. They came perhaps from countries where they had never at any time exercised the franchise, and consequently did not appreciate the privilege that was given to them. I contend that before any person secures the franchise they should have an intelligent grasp of what the franchise means.

A negress comes to Canada with an American husband. The American husband is naturalized, and she is therefore entitled to vote. A French woman from Paris, highly educated, comes over with her husband. The husband is naturalized a British subject. This woman has no vote, while the negress has. Does my hon. friend think that fair?

It may possibly be that there are some anomalies in the working of the law, but I would point out that the whole principle of the Franchise Bill is to extend the franchise. By this Bill we are not taking away from anybody anything they now have, but are simply extending the franchise to some. We are extending a means by which these people can exercise the franchise if they comply with certain conditions. My hon. friend (Mr.	Cannon) said that the
Bill as it stands is not generous enough. My hon. friend- the Acting Solicitor General has agreed to an enlargement by the amendment which he proposes, and I think that in that regard he has done well. I for one would not advocate that we should enter into any reactionary policy in connection with the franchise. I think we must be broad and generous in the construction of our franchise law. Nevertheless, Sir, I believe that it is the duty of this Parliament to safeguard the Tights conferred by the franchise so that this greatest privilege of citizenship may be exercised wisely and intelligently. I wish to point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Cannon) that he is not quite consistent, because, if I mistake not, there is in some of the provinces of Canada to-day a property qualifica-

tion for voters. In other words, the principle which he enunciates, namely, that the fact of your being a British subject entitles you to vote provided you are twenty-one years of age and can comply with certain other requirements, is not applicable generally throughout the country. In provincial matters, there are property qualifications in some of the provinces. I think that Nova Scotia a few years ago, if not to-day, had such qualifications, and it is not many years ago since the other provinces had them. Generally speaking, we have passed that stage in the Dominion arena; we have virtually reached the point of universal franchise, although there are some classes that are still restricted, and I think Mr. Chairman that we are exceedingly wise in imposing the restrictions that exist. And I am reminded-I intended to state the fact-that these restrictions are imposed upon persons who are undoubtedly British subjects in every sense of the term. We enforce in a very marked sense the resident qualification. A man must have been for a certain time resident in the electoral district in which he votes. He might have been born in this country and have lived here all his life; he might have been prime minister of a province for a dozen years; but if he has not been a resident in the electoral district for a stated period he cannot vote. We look upon that as a necessary qualification, and this and other restrictions are eminently wise, notwithstanding that they apply to British subjects bom or naturalized. The point I am driving at is simply this, that you cannot lay down the principle that because a person is a British subject either by birth or by naturalization he therefore necessarily is entitled to the franchise. The franchise is a right that exists altogether independently of the naturalization law, and in this Act we are not violating that law at all. We are dealing with a separate matter which is of the greatest importance in itself, and so long as this Act deals fairly with the people of the country and gives them a reasonable opportunity to exercise the franchise it discharges the function which is supposed to attach to it.
I desire to say a word or two in regard to the disfranchisement of certain classes of people. Now, Sir, I feel very strongly with the hon. member for Red Deer and one or two other hon. gentlemen whom I have heard speak on this question, that we should as early as possible in Canada allay the bitterness that has been engendered

by the late war and endeavour to establish a new relation with our enemies. That is desirable, and I should be the last person to say anything now that might tend to open old wounds. But, Mr. Chairman, while we entertain that feeling-and I think it is genuinely entertained throughout the country-nevertheless there are certain things which common sense demands that we shall recognize. Although perhaps a large proportion of the people disfranchised by reason of enemy alien origin may wish to be good and loyal citizens of this country, still we have had ample experience to know that there are designing persons who even to-day, after all the bitter lessons of the war, are quite willing to use their influence among this class of people to the detriment of the country. We cannot shut our eyes to that fact; I do not think we dare. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I would be the last man to stir up any rancour or ill feeling, but the fact must be apparent that-
Mr. (HI. A. MACKIE:	Would the hon.
gentleman mind naming the agitators who are creating tne disturbances or who .are bringing any influence to bear on people in this country?	,

-it is obvious, Mr. Chairman, that I am speaking in a general sense, and I think my hon. friend knows that perfectly well. But it would be entirely beside the question for me to mention any names at this time.

Does the hon. gentleman
not know that in such cases as he has referred to it would be the duty of the judge to examine the persons who appeared before him and to decide whether they were woithy of naturalization, and that if he found that they were not worthy he would be in duty bound to refuse the credentials?
I presume the hon. gentleman is referring to this clause under discussion?
Exactly.

Well, let me say that I am supporting the clause and I agree with my hon. friend so far as this clause is concerned. But what I do say-I think it is well that I should repeat it, and I can assure hon. gentlemen that I have no desire whatever to stir up troubl.e-is that it is unwise for us to close our eyes to the fact that there are individuals in Canada to-day who are quite willing to . exploit the bitter feelings that arose during
the late war in order to create discord and trouble in the country. The same thing has been experienced to the south of us, perhaps to a greater extent than in Canada. So that in the framing of this Franchise Bill, Parliament must take care that it shall not carelessly or recklessly extend the privilege of the franchise. One other point, Mr. Chairman, and I shall conclude. As years go by these disabilities which we have, as I think, very wisely imposed may be removed as present unsettled conditions subside and become normal once more, but I do not think that it is wise at this time to go to any extreme that may involve us in danger.

I do not purpose to discuss the question of the disfranchisement of certain British subjects, because I am well satisfied with what the minister said last night, if I understood him correctly. He said:
The object of the present amendment is to make definite and certain that every one who is actually a British subject shall enjoy the right to vote, and if the amendment that I have moved does not make that clear, we shall make it clear if a better method can be suggested.
I assume that the minister was referring to cases of the kind under discussion: that is, the wives and families of naturalized British subjects from alien countries. I think I can quite' agree with him in that, if he is prepared to change his amendment in such a way as to carry out what he says he has in mind.
In one or two respects the amendment as drawn will not, in my opinion, accomplish what I assume the minister desires to accomplish ; and I assume he desires to accomplish what he says he desires. The wives and children of naturalized Germans and Austrians in our country are, in cases where the husband or father is naturalized, British subjects. I assume that my hon. friend's desire is to give all these people the right to vote; if he does not mean that, his statement of last night will require a good deal of explanation. Anything I have to say in this discussion will be with a view to directing the minister's attention to some things which I believe would prevent him from carrying out his desires as expressed last night. In the first place, the applicant for certificate must show that he or she is of good character and has an adequate knowledge of the English or French language. That is not the most important matter on which I wish to speak, but let me dwell upon it for a moment. I think I

am right in saying that the section as proposed to be amended by the minister *will mean that every person applying to a judge for a certificate such as is required under the section must satisfy 'that judge that he or she has a good knowledge of English or French and is of good character. Now the ghod character requirement we can hardly object to. In a great many cases, however, wives of naturalized British subjects will be debarred on the language test. Is that the minister's intention? The amendment means that any barrier placed upon a person by reason of section 8 of the Naturalization Act shall not disentitle him or her to receive that certificate from the judge. Has it occurred to the minister that in order to carry out the spirit of the Act the judge must in many cases give an absolutely false certificate? He must certify that the person is a person naturalized by operation of law, who, but for such naturalization "is qualified and would be entitled at the issue of this certificate to be personally naturalized in Canada." Now, the wife or child of a naturalized German or Austrian would not be qualified under these circumstances and would not be so entitled to naturalization. While the spirit of the amendment proposed would, perhaps, justify the judge in granting that quasi false certificate, I am satisfied that I know a judge who will hot grant it under the circumstances; he will not give the certificate to the wife ot the child of a German or an Austrian. I would not blame him for that, because we have no right to ask a judge to issue what is evidently a false certificate, even though it may be in keeping with the spirit of the. law. What are you going to do with the judge who, on that ground, refuses to issue the certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That brings us to the point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Euler). My view is, and I am pretty strong in it, that the certificate is right in the form in which it appears in the Bill. The member for North Waterloo does not take that iew; he doubts whether that is correct. Mr. Mulvey, the Under-Secretary of State, who has the administration of the Naturalization Act, is also inclined to think that there may be some doubt, and if a judge in the West has cast a doubt upon it, there is all the more reason why it should be made clear. Mr. Mulvey suggests that it can be made clear by inserting two or three words in the certificate, and when
{Mr. Thomson.]
we come to it I propose to move an amendment.

I would like the minister to note the objection that I have taken; I do not know whether it is the same as that made by the hon. member for North Waterloo.
There is another point. Those who have had to do with naturalization know that the foreigner, as we call him, is not likely to apply for naturalization until he has some particular object in view, until there is some particular reason for his doing so. My experience is not exactly in line with what the member for Regina (Mr. Cowman) says' was his experience and that of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder). I know that in the old days a great many of these people used to apply for naturalization before an election. In fact, that was about the only time they wanted it, unless it was when they wanted their patents. Now, what will be the result of that practice under present conditions? Large numbers of these 'people will not bother about this certificate until they are pretty sure an election is coming on, and in some of our western districts the judges will have their hands full if they properly carry out the idea which, I take it, the minister has in mind. I assume that the minister will expect the judge to require those who go before him for this purpose to establish that they are able to read and write the English or the French languages and also that they are of good character. How is the judge to satisfy himself 'on the point of character? I do not know what the rule followed by all the judges in the West is, but in the Moosomin district a judge, when he wants to satisfy himself as to the character of an applicant, must have before him two persons who know the applicant and whom the judge also knows. He will pay no attention to any person coming to swear as to the character of the applicant unless it is some one whom he himself knows. These applications must be made only before him in chambers at Moosomin. Now the judicial district of Moosomin is one of the oldest and most densely populated districts of Saskatchewan, and many of these people live seventy-five or eighty miles from the town of Moosomin itself. The requirement seems to be that such persons must go to Moosomin with two witnesses who must know the applicants, and must be known to the judge. With these special persons to vouch for them the applicants must go all that

distance, in each case we will say, to Moosomin. Now there are a great many of such people that will require those certificates and the time of the judge will be pretty well occupied in hearing these applications. I would like the minister-sometime later, when he is on his feet-to relieve my mind as to whether there would be any limitation on the right of the judge to make a ruling as to the evidence that must be submitted before him, as to the persons by whom it shall be submitted, and also as to where the hearings can take place. It seems to me that there can be no proper reason why the judge should not be able to hear those applications at any place where he holds a district court. Even that would not be very satisfactory, for the reason that in most of the places. outside of the judicial centra court is only held twice a year; and when an election is in view, at the time these people would be coming forward with their applications, there is no district court being held at that particular place and the parties desirous of making the application would either have to go to Moosomin or abandon their purpose altogether. If the section is passed, with the amendment suggested, a very large proportion of these people will be British subjects by operation of law- that is the wives and children of naturalized persons who were former Germans or Austrians-but only a very small number of them would be qualified to vote when an election takes place.
I would also make one further suggestion to my hon. friend who states that he is willing to receive suggestions-whether it is advisable or not I leave to himself-if he insists on some such certificate being granted, would it not be possible to have some persons appointed for this purpose in each important town or village throughout the district? For instance, take my own district, if half a dozen or a dozen men at the most important points were given the right to issue those certificates I would be quite willing to allow' my hon. friend to appoint those men himself, because, in my opinion, he will choose men that are honest and thoroughly reliable. Let such persons as those issue the certificates. They know far more about the character of the applicants than the judge possibly could. After all that is the important point, and I think my hon. friend will agree with me as to that-such persons will be in a very much better position to give a certificate than any judge would. Therefore I would like my hon. friend to consider that suggestion.

It has been stated this afternoon by the Acting Solicitor General-and reference to it has been made by the member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon)-that this amendment has come as a result of certain representations I made some time ago, and the minister intimated that the amendment was in some sense to meet my wishes. That may be true. So far as I am concerned I feel that the amendment which has been submitted, and which we are now discussing does, in a measure, meet the views that were placed before the House at that time. But I was rather surprised to hear the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cannon) state that it has absolutely no effect in the direction desired. If that were the case I would say, either that the w'ork of the man who drafted the amendment is very bad, or that the amendment is an attempt at the w'orst betrayal of which any Government could possibly be guilty. I would hesitate to believe either of these conclusions; I do not view the amendment in that way.
I do not want to be placed in the position of opposing the amendment because I am in favour of it so far as it goes; my only objection to it is that it does not go quite far enough. It must be apparent to every member who has followed the course of this debate that a great deal of confusion exists as to exactly what the clause and the amendment mean. I am pretty sure that at least ninety per cent of the members of the House do not yet appreciate the distinction-and this is casting no reflection on any hon. member-that should be made between those people that are not naturalized and who we think should be allowed the franchise by naturalization, and that other group of people who were discussed on the second reading of the Bill, and whose grievance this amendment is supposed to remedy. I am not now going to discuss the status of those who are not British subjects. I shall do what I did the other night -refer to the rights of those women and men who are actually naturalized British subjects, and who, in my opinion, should be given the vote without being put to the necessity of going before a judge and once again proving that they are entitled to, and are fit persons to exercise the franchise. Now if the whole question has i.een so confusing to the members of the House, it is not to be wondered at if the same condition exists throughout the country, and it will certainly exist in the minds of the people who are most intimately affected by the condition in question. But I submit, Sir, that it is entirely unnecessary that

any such confusion should exist. This amendment is not the best that could be offered. The existing contusion will vanish if we simply follow the law as we have it already in the Naturalization Act, entirely apart from this clause and which a much simpler amendment will accomplish. The whole difficulty, to my mind, arises from the fact that an attempt is here being made to enact a law which is in direct contradiction to the law which already appears on the statute books of Canada. When the Government realized the unfortunate effects of the proposed new law, they undertook to remedy the defect-not by removing the clause which is in direct opposition to an established principle of law already on the statute books of Canada, but by trying to reconcile two irreconcilable things, and thus they complicated and confused the whole question more than ever. I believe, Sir, that is stating the absolute fact. The whole difficulty arises by trying to enact a law which will be in direot contradiction to a law which already exists, and nothing but confusion can result from such an attempt.
First, we have the principle laid down in the Naturalization Act, that the wife of a British subject is herself a British subject. We may regard that, I think, as a definite axiom. It is not only enacted in the naturalization law of 1919, but it has been affirmed in every previous naturalization law since Confederation. Therefore I say it is an accepted axiom that the wife of a British subject is herself a British subject.
Then, quite inconsistently, hi subsection 2 of section 29 we say in plain English that in so far as voting is concerned she is not a British subject. That is the extraordinary statement in that paragraph. In our naturalization law we say that the wife of *a British subject is a British subject; but in this proposed election law we say in so many words that she is not a British subject. The two terms are absolutely contradictory, and that is why the confusion arises.
Now, when the difficulty is noted, along comes this amendment which tries to reconcile what I submit are two unreconcilable things. How can a person be a British subject and yet not be a British subject?
In my opinion, Sir, the remedy is very ' plain. Choose which of the two principles -the one already in the Naturalization Act under which the wife of a British subject is herself a British subject; and the other principle enunciated in this Franchise Act, that she is not a British sub-

ject for the purpose of voting-I say choose which of these two principles is the right one, and then destroy the one that is wrong. That seems to me to be the logical course to follow.
These women and these men who, as minors, became naturalized by operation of law are British subjects, as has been pointed out again and again, and I assert that it is absurd to say that right here in Canada-where after all this Parliament should have full control-those men and women shall be British subjects for one purpose and not for another; that for example, the men shall be put in the dual characters of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde: The whole thing is an absurdity and should not be placed upon the statute books.
Might I ask the hon. member a question? How would he treat British subjects who come to this country from British India?

That is a very easy question for me to answer. I would say that a person who is a British subject in Canada should be given the vote, regardless of colour, creed or racial origin. That is my personal opinion.
As I said before, Mr. Chairman, these women are British subjects and their husbands are British subjects. I declare, and I know something of what I am about to say, that these husbands are probably no better and no worse than their wives so far as fitness for the franchise is concerned. These men, and quite properly so, are now permitted to cast their ballots, though of alien origin. Then the franchise having been extended to our 'Women, and quite properly so, why should it not follow that as these men are granted the franchise, their wives-who are just as much British subjects as their husbands-should also be granted the franchise? Why should they be put under the necessity and the humiliation of going before a judge and showing once again that they are fit and proper persons to be given the franchise?

Will the hon. member permit me a question? He speaks of the wives going before a judge and showing once again that they are fit and proper persons to exercise the franchise. Is it not true that they have never before shown that fitness, nor have they ever established that they have the qualifications which their husbands had to have in order to be granted naturalization? And while I am on my feet, let me ask another question. Before the husbands could secure 'the fran-

chise they had to comply with the Naturalization Act; the women never were naturalized under that Act, but by law, which law was 'based upon certain principles before women were enfranchised. Now that women are enfranchised, is it not fair that these wives should be asked to qualify up to the standard of their husbands?

The hon. gentleman tries to introduce a principle that has never been introduced before. The franchise has now been given to all women who are British subjects, except this particular class of whom we are speaking. There has been no intimation given that the Government is going to make certain that
5 p.m. other' women are to be tested before a judge as to whether they are fit and proper persons to exercise the franchise. If we are going to be consistent, Mr. Chairman, if we are going to make these people who have lived in the country for many years, to say nothing of the men who have voted in past years, and whom you are now going to make go before a judge to show their fitness to exercise the franchise-if we are going to do that, we should make certain that everybody who in future casts his ballot is a fit and proper person to be granted that privilege. Why not go back and make every woman who will now vote show that she is a fit and proper person to cast the ballot? Why confine it to the alien-born if the present law as to naturalization is to be satisfied? It seems to me that that is the only logical course to take if you want to be consistent. I contend that to-day there are men in this country-and many women too, who could not possibly fulfil the requirements of the Naturalization Act, as it is at this moment. Are we going to shut them out from the vote? We are not, and I think it is quite Tight that that we do not, because it would be a mistake to make that provision retroactive in respect to a privilege which they already have. The alien-born British subject should not be discriminated against.
I contended last evening that this law should not be made to apply to people who are already living in this country and are British subjects, but that, if desired, we might apply this law to those who come here in the future. They come then with their eyes open, knowing what is expected of them. I for one iam quite in sympathy with the principle that in future, men and women alike, should be made to show that they are fit subjects for naturalization, and thus for the franchise.
Peculiarly enough, I have not heard any real defence of this subsection 2 of section 29 or any real reason given for its adoption. No real argument has been adduced as to why these women in particular should be segregated from their husbands, than whom they are no better and no worse-perhaps the wives are a little better; I am willing to admit that. Then why should they be put to the necessity of going before a judge and proving that they are fit persons to vote? I have heard no argument that convinces me of the necessity for this provision; in fact, all hon. members on the other side who have spoken, have practically avoided that point.
I was alluding a few moments ago to the fact that a great deal of confusion exists, and I listened with approval to what was said by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Levi Thomson). He stated that in his opinion the inclusion of this paragraph in the Bill will result, in a practical way, in the disfranchisement of a great proportion of these people. In that I think he is absolutely correct. I gave some of the reasons for my belief last night. In the first place, many of these women, especially those who are aged-and many of them are elderly women-will absolutely refuse to go through the ordeal of appearing before a judge and submitting themselves to a series of questions. Thqy will prefer to remain at home and lose their vote. It may be said that that is not the proper attitude on their part; but it is a very natural one. On the other hand, I think a great many of these people, particularly the men, may be placed upon the voters' lists by those who think they ought to be there legally, and perhaps placed there by others who think that they have a moral right to be there- a great many of these people, knowing that their names are on the voters' lists, will go to no further trouble to get the certificate required by law, and when they appear at the polling booth they may be challenged by those opposed to them politically with the result that they will be deprived of their votes. I believe that will be the practical result of the inclusion of this clause in the Bill. All the confusion, all the injustice and all danger from a wrong interpretation of the Act; all danger that a judge even may make a partisan use of his power, and refuse the certificate to perfectly worthy people, British subjects, will disappear, if you will take the law as it stands to-day in the Naturalization Act and say that when a person is a British subject, he is -a British

subject for all purposes, including the franchise, if he fulfils the other requirements. As I said last night, I believe earnestly if a man or a woman is of the age of twenty-one years and is of good character, he or she should have the franchise as the direct result of British citizenship, and this clause which imposes on those people the necessity of going before a judge and proving to his satisfaction- and perhaps failing to prove to his satisfaction-that they are fit and proper persons to exercise the franchise, should be struck out.
Surely this should appeal to the Government as the only logical, fair and reasonable way in which to cure the wrong that flowed out of the Act as it was originally framed. I should like to press home on the Acting Solicitor General and the Government that by so doing they will be the means of saving many worthy people from difficulties and inconveniences which they do not deserve to have placed upon them. Believing that, I shall move an amendment to the amendment of the Acting Solicitor General and I hope he will accept it and withdraw his own, because I believe my amendment will meet the sense of fairness of most of the people of this country when they know the facts free from misrepresentation. I move in amendment to the amendment:
That subclause 2 of clause 29 of the Bill be struck out in its entirety.

The
legal effect of the Franchise Bill as now proposed has been given very well this afternoon by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) and other hon. gentlemen, but I believe they have exaggerated to a certain degree the evils which may crop up under this measure. The amendment to the amendment undoubtedly meets the situation which both the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Euler) and myself had the honour of suggesting to the House on the second reading, and if hon. gentlemen opposite will take the trouble to study the amendment to the amendment carefully, they will see that it meets that situation. I said on that occasion that the Government can have only one purpose for that clause, namely, that it desires to raise the standard of the voter. My hon. friend (Mr. Euler) has, I believe, struck the proper key-note this afternoon along with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. L. Thomson), when they say that, whereas you are endeavouring to raise that standard by this legislation, you are making
fMr. Euler.]
it possible, first, that persons applying for a certificate will be denied that certificate by reason of the prejudice unfortunately existing at present in the country, and second, that those who will be denied a certificate because they do not come up to the qualifications required of them under the Naturalization Act, shall be deprived of casting a vote in the elections in this country when, as a matter of fact, there are, in Western Canada as well as in Eastern Canada, very many persons who have to ask their friends in the polling booth how to mark their ballots. I am entirely in accord with the motive of the Government, and I do not believe the accusations of hon. gentlemen, opposite against the Government are well founded. I am entirely in accord with the desire of the Government to establish a higher standard of education in the matter of voting, but I believe this is not the proper occasion on which to deal with that matter. I would rather see a law which would contain a provision stating that hereafter unless you can speak or write the English or the French language, or unless you have an adequate knowledge of one or the other or both languages, you may not vote. Then, we would have the whole population on an equal footing. I know, for instance, that in the western provinces there are a large number of men and women who will not be able to get their certificates, not because of their fault, but because of the circumstances in which they are situated and of their age, it will be impossible for them to qualify unless a judge is willing to take the broad view that he used to take at a time when such men came before him for naturalization papers for the purpose of securing patents to land. Under those circumstances, a judge was lenient, because he realized that it was necessary for a man to get his naturalization papers for the purpose of getting patent to his land. If such a man could say a few words in English or French and could express the balance of his meaning by gesticulation with his hands or by some otiher method, the judge would say: All right, I will give you your naturalization papers. But when such a man comes before a judge to obtain qualification to vote the judge may not be so lenient, and I know of some judges who have refused -such people naturalization right along. Even now I have received letters from some of my constituents stating that they have made application and that they have been turned down because they do not know enough' of the English lan-

guage. This is one method of disfranchising those people, and they should not be treated in this way, unless you go further and treat every one in the same manner. What about the half-breed population we have in Western Canada? I attended one poll at Fort Chippewyan where there were 90 voters, not one of whom himself marked his ballot, but whose ballot was marked for him by the deputy returning officer when they told him for whom they wanted to vote. I doubt if they understood the issues in the" provincial election; but they were entitled to vote, althought in the light of this provision in this Franchise Bill, they would not be permitted to vote.
Another feature which I should like to discuss for a moment is this. In Western Canada, there is a large population from Galicia. One portion of Galicia has to-day passed under the dominance of Poland; the other portion has been separated from Austria, but it does not belong to any country in particular, except that Poland has been given a sort of mandate temporarily until the League of Nations decides the issue whether eastern Galicia shall go into independent Ukraine or whether it shall form part of Russia as a whole. These people in the meantime are being looked upon as alien enemies, as Austrians, although they are detached from the Austrian Empire, and all of those people, by reason of the fact that the League of Nations has not yet determined what country they are in future to be nationals of have been refused naturalization papers. I have a number of letters from the Under-Secretary of State stating definitely that these people would be refused their naturalization papers until such time as the League of Nations shall decide where they belong. Assuming that this Government will finish the terms and that two more years will elapse before an election takes place, if the League of Nations shall have settled by that time the destiny of these people, they will then be entitled to make application for naturalization. If not, there will be out West a very large number of people who will not be able to vote at all, because they cannot be naturalized in Canada for the purpose of acquiring citizenship, and certainly they cannot be naturalized for the purpose of voting.
I would point out the advisability of supporting the amendment to the amendment and treating these people on the broad lines we have been accustomed to in the past in dealing with all the people of this Dominion. If there is to be any high standard of citizenship required before a vote can
be cast let the Act state, that from now on certain classes shall not be allowed to help to determine public questions in Canada unless they have a certain educational status. I would support such a proposal if it were made to apply to all alike. But at the present time I should think that we are discriminating, because we are allowing a large number of people to vote who have no greater learning or education than those from foreign countries who have been brought to the western provinces. Let a standard be fixed from now on; let there be no discrimination. I would also ask the Acting Solicitor General to take into consideration the fact that in the three western provinces that large population from Galicia will not be able to secure the franchise unless the League of Nations decides within the next two years what shall happen to them.

I feel as if I were playing a return engagement here this afternoon, because I was the last to speak on this question last night. But I cannot allow the question to be put to a vote without saying a final word in the hope that the Acting Solicitor General may have had his heart softened in the meantime. This matter is of vital importance to the people in the large cities, where, we have, as the House knows, an exceptionally lafge foreign population. I said last night that I estimated there were at least 5,000 of these foreign born people in my division who would be affected by this Bill. In the other divisions of Montreal there are at least as many, so that in the city of Montreal we have 10,000 foreign born who will be affected by this legislation. Last night when I asked the Acting Solicitor General why he sought to introduce this distinction into our law, he said:
Because we recognize that people born on this continent are very similar in their ideas, laws, customs and habits to our own people and we can very quickly assimilate them to our ways.
That being the case you would expect that a judge who was going to pass on the applications brought before him would look into the question whether the applicant's ideas, laws, customs and habits were similar to ours or otherwise. Let me invite your attention to the form provided in section 29:
This is to certify that from evidence submitted before me 1 am satisfied that A. B. of	in the province of...(occupation)	is a person naturalized as a
British subject by operation of law, who, but for such naturalization, is qualified and would

be entitled at the date of the issue of this certificate to he personally naturalized in Canada.
Is there anything said there with regard to the ideas, laws, customs, habits and character of the applicant? Not a word. The object of this certificate, as can be seen from the form, is identification pure and simple, and I challenge the Acting Solicitor General to show me where it applies to anything outside of identification. Why should the judges of the high court in the city of Montreal, for instance, be put to the trouble and inconvenience and annoyance of merely passing upon a question of identification when that could be [DOT]very well done by the enumerator 'or by the deputy returning officer?
I say that the object of this section is to prevent as many as possible of the foreign born from voting at the next election. That is the object, camouflage it as you may, and I challenge the Acting Solicitor General to say that it is for any other object. He spoke of the ideas, law, customs and habits of our people, and contrasted them with those of the people coming here from Europe. Does the Acting Solicitor General know that under this Act people from Mexico, from Haiti, and from the Central American republics will have the right to vote? Every negress, every mulatto, and evfiry quadroon in the United States who comes here and marries a British subject will have the right to vote. In what way I should like to know will that contribute to elevating our ideas, our customs, and character, and habits, and the mental and moral welfare of the people of this country? The women from Belgium and France, many of whom took part in'the war, are not to be allowed this privilege but have to submit to this humiliating application which the minister intends to thrust upon them. I admire consistency and frankness in any one, as much in a government as in a private individual, and I say it is rank hypocrisy on the part of the Government to attempt to tell us that tlie object of this law is to see to it that the people who are voting under this law conform to the customs and ideas of the native born.
I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that when the Military Voters' Act was put on the statute books there was no such wild attempt to see to it that the ideas, the customs and habits and morality of the women who voted under that Act should be as carefully investigated as they are supposed to be under this Act. Women

voters under that Act were taken wherever they could be found. If a man in the trenches had nine or ten sisters at home, he had eleven votes, no matter whether the women were from Belgium or France or Timbuctoo. The Government needed those votes, and they made use of them. Today they think they do not need them. In fact in a very negative way, they do not need them because the Government knows how the women are going to vote so they bring before Parliament a measure to see that as few as possible will vote at the next election. This giving the vote to the women and then taking it away from them is very much in line with a good many other so-called philanthropic acts of the Government, but when you examine it you find you have very little. It is another case of, the Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away, but in this case we cannot say, Blessed be the name of the Lord. I would like to have the Acting Solicitor General pinned down to a statement regarding the form attached to section 29, and to ascertain from him how a judge by giving a certificate identifying a party as the party entitled to vote is going to give us any assurance as to the character of the voter. The thing is absurd. It is simply another piece of hypocrisy on the part of the Government, who under the guise of seeing to it that the people who come to this country are respectable and law-abiding citizens are depriving many of their right to exercise the franchise which they would have, but for this section.
I cannot add anything to what I have already said on this matter. When the By-elections Bill was before the House in July, 1919, I opposed it as vigorously as I couid. When the Naturalization Act was before the House I opposed it, I opposed this Bill on its second reading and I intend to oppose it at every turn until it finally becomes law and as I hinted last night I intend to oppose it even then. The Government, I fear, in its own interests is making a mistake in attempting to place on the statute books laws of this kind. After all, what reason have they to feel that all these women whom it is sought to prevent from voting at the next election are going to vote against them? The Government claim that at the last election about 250,000 or 300,000 women voted for them. How is it that such a change has come about in the mentality of the women of this country? It is said that women sometimes, by intuition know who are their friends and who are not; and probably the Government

has come to the conclusion that the women are going to vote against them en masse on that account. In this Bill there is a distinction which ought not to exist. We do not want to have one law for the stranger and another law for the British born subject. The law that exists in the land should be the law for all persons who live in the land, and any attempt to derogate or deviate from that well established principle is bound to meet with the reprobation of the citizens of this country. The Government may think that they are going to succeed by putting on the statute book a law of this kind, but I warn them that it will recoil upon their heads. There are a large number of foreign born people who will be permitted to vote under this Act, but their relatives will be precluded from the privilege, and I want to warn the Government seriously, that many of these people whose relatives are to be prohibited from voting at the next election are certainly not going to cast their votes in favour of a Government that puts on the statute book of the country a measure as iniquitous as this one.

Will the minister be
kind enough to tell me what good reason there is and what good purpose will be served by compelling these British subjects to travel miles from their homes to obtain certificates? I represent in this House a purely rural constituency in which there is not a judicial centre, and the women who will be affected in that constituency will have to travel many miles at great expense, and will be absent from their families for one or more nights if they desire to obtain the necessary certificate. The law says that these people are British subjects. It gives to their husbands, who are British subjects, the right of the franchise, and I cannot see any good reason why these women should be compelled to apply to a judge or any tribunal for a certificate. Will the minister be kind enough to make a statement in regard to that point?
Will the hon. gentleman say who he thinks will grant the certificate if not the judge?
I have asked the minister a question and I should like to have an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The question asked by the hon. member is practically the same as one submitted by the hon. member for Qu'Ap-peile. Under this Bill as drawn it is provided that a person who has become a British subject by operation of law, in order to 134
vote, shall obtain a certificate from a judge. That certificate is not for the purpose of identity, as my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier suggested a few moments ago; it is for the purpose of satisfying the judge that the woman has such qualifications that in any event, though she niay be a British subject by operation of law, she would be entitled to naturalization. I do not know the riding which my hon. friend represents, but I know that under this Act it is not only one circuit judge that can give a certificate. Any of the Superior Court judges can give it, and I assume that courts are held at regular intervals in these outlying districts. In the dense settlement of Montreal, according to my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs), some ten thousand women will have to procure certificates, but I am satisfied even that large number can be accommodated for there are some thirty or forty judges in Montreal who will have the power to grant these certificates. One can easily magnify the difficulties under this Act, and no doubt there will be some inconvenience imposed. It has been pointed out that some judges may take exceptional views of the matter. Well, we are supposed to have judges who will take reasonable views of the law and administer the law as it stands; and I think that if there are judges who will not do so their conduct should be reported to the proper authorities. I cannot understand that any judge would say: "I will hear applications only at one point in my district." There is nothing in the Act that limits his jurisdiction in any way; there is nothing that imposes such a limitation upon him. I think myself that the judge is bound to hear an application wherever it is made, in any part of the territory under his jurisdiction, and I see nothing to prevent any judge from any other part of the province from coming in. This can be done in Ontario.
Is that true in regard to an application for naturalization? Is the judge bound to hear an application for naturalization from any point?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The judge is bound by the language of this statute, and there is nothing to say that he will hear applications only in one particular place. He must hear them wherever they are made in the territory over which he has jurisdiction, and there is nothing in this law that says he can name particular places.

The minister has not caught my question. I want to know



if the same thing applies to an application for naturalization. Is the judge bound to hear that application at any place; if not, what is the distinction?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think he is hound to hear it at any place. The application has to be filed, in the case of naturalization, in the office of the clerk of the court. In this case the judge has jurisdiction over every portion of his territory, and it is not for him to say that he will hear applications only in this or the other place, and if a judge takes that ground his conduct should be reported to the proper authorities, and I am satisfied he would not continue in such a course or the law would speedily be changed.
Will any fee be charged for the certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, there is no fee for the certificate. I do not know that I can give any further information to the committee. I know that there are two views in regard 'to this amendment as there probably are in regard to the original clause. My hon. friend from Dorchester took forty minutes this afternoon to denounce my amendment and to show that it was, in his opinion, absolutely worthless. Yet my hon. friend from North Waterloo approved of it; he evidently thinks that half a loaf is better than no bread.
I thank the minister for expressing the very thought I had in mind. I was just about to say the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As I said last night and repeat now, if there is anything uncertain about the amendment which my hon. friend can make clearer by other language I am willing to give every consideration to his suggestions. If the language of the Undersecretary of State meets the views of my hon. friend we may consider it. The amendment I have submitted meets with the approval of the Government, and it is the desire that it be passed.

In my riding there is a judicial centre and the resident district judge hold, sittings of the district court throughout that territory. Suppose an application is filed with the court in one part of that territory and the judge is sitting somewhere else, could the party who filed the application appear before the judge where he is sitting and ask for the certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Undoubtedly.

I understood
my hon. friend (Mr. L. Thomson) to say that a similar request had been refused in his constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Then the matter had
better be referred to the proper authorities.
It has always been believed that judges of this country hold office for the convenience of the public as well as for the administration of law. If they get the other idea into their heads, the sooner we pass some law on the subject the better.

Subsection 2 of clause 29 states:
For the purposes of this Act, the allegiance or nationality of a person, as it was at the birth of such person, shall be deemed incapable of being changed ... by reason of .	.	.	.
naturalization of any other person or otherwise than by personal naturalization.
Now, section 33 of the Naturalization Act reads, in part:
Where in pursuance of this Act the name of a child is included in a certificate of naturalization granted to his parent, or where, in pursuance of any Act repealed by this Act, any child has been deemed to be a naturalized British subject by reason of residence with his parent, such child shall, for the purposes of this Act, be deemed to be a person to whom a certificate of naturalization has been granted.
Under the Naturalization Act of 1919 a minor child becomes a British subject on account of the naturalization of his father and is deemed to be personally naturalized; is deemed to have received a certificate of naturalization. How do you reconcile the two Acts?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
He gets it by operation
of law. He does not actually get a certificate.

He is deemed to have
had a certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the operation
of law; that is what is referred to. He gets no actual certificate, but by operation of law he becomes a British subject and is deemed to have received a certificate.

I think my hon. friend is not right as to that. The wife becomes a British subject by operation of law. There is no section that says the wife is deemed to have received the certificate. Minor children are placed in the same situation as the wife; they are deemed to be naturalized by the operation of law, but there is a special section which states that they are considered as having been personally naturalized, as having themselves received certificate of naturalization. How can you reconcile these two provisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
They never have been
personally naturalized and they never have received a certificate. The law says they shall be deemed to have been personally naturalized; consequently it is by operation of law that they are such.

That only serves to
show the absurdity of legislation which makes persons half British subjects and half aliens. If personal naturalization is required of a person in order that he may be a British subject, then change the naturalization law. I read in an American magazine some days ago an article which stated that changes in the naturalization law of United States are being advocated to provide that personal naturalization only shall be valid. Change the law if you like, but as long as the naturalization of the husband carries with it the naturalization of the wife, the wife should be deemed a British subject for all purposes, not for some purposes only. People seem to be under the impression that this provision is designed only to meet the case of persons whose parents were of enemy origin. Well, that is a mistake; this provision applies also to persons coming from friendly countries. As was stated this afternoon, persons of French, Italian and Belgian descent, persons from other countries which were associated with Great Britain in the war, even though they are British subjects by the naturalization of husbands or fathers, would, under this provision, be deprived of the right to vote. This is a point of view which should be considered before section 29 is adopted in its present form. We have the disability clause providing for the ten year period of disfranchisement because that provision was first enacted by the British Parliament. The British electoral law never required personal naturalization on the part of women to entitle them to vote. Under the Representation of the People Act, 1918, women who are British subjects by birth or by naturalization are entitled to vote. Why should we have any different provision in this country? It is arbitrary to ask people to get a certificate from a judge before they shall have the right to vote. The right to vote should be made clear by Act of Parliament; it should not 'be subject to the whim of any person, a judge or any one else. Judges have very-ing rules in connection with the application of laws, especially when it is a question of administration, as will be the case under this Act. Some judges are more strict than others; some insist upon the furnishing of more particulars by applicants than others 134*
do. The law will not be uniform In its application, and for that reason and for all the other reasons that have been given this afternoon, I shall support the amendment of my hon. friend from North Waterloo.

Mr. Chairman, as I understand it, all these new troubles and difficulties that we have in connection with the franchise arose out of the war. We had no such difficulties before the war. Any man who came to this country obtained his naturalization, and there was no further trouble about it-he was entitled to all the privileges of a British subject. For that reason I cannot see why troubles which have arisen out of the war should be visited upon those nations which were friendly to us and fought side by side with us during the conflict, and why we should, by reason of the disturbing elements of war conditions, place at a disadvantage and disfranchise all these people who were friends and allies in the struggle. That is something I cannot very well understand. I notice, 'Sir, that in subclause (B), of subclause 4 of section eight of the Naturalization Act that we passed last year that when we were to inflict punishment upon a certain class of people we confined that arrangement to our enemies during th- war. The subclause referred to states:
No certificate of naturalization shall, wfore the expiration of a period of ten years after the termination of the present war, be granted in Canada to any subject of a country which at the time of the passing of this Act was at war with His Majesty, but this provision shall not apply to a person whoand so forth. The idea of subclause (B) is to inflict that punishment and that disability upon subjects of a country who opposed us in the war. What I cannot understand is this: If an Italian came to this country to-day he would not require to be here ten years before he got naturalization; he got it in the ordinary way and perhaps he was never in the country before. But there may be an Italian woman who has been in Canada for perhaps twenty years. Our law ordinarily confers the franchise upon women; but that Italian woman will not be permitted to vote unless she goes perhaps a distance of sixty or seventy miles, states her case to a judge, and from that judge obtains a certificate. I submit, Sir, that the Acting Solicitor General should particularly consider that phase of the case. I am unable to understand why this disability has been placed upon friendly-foreigners, if you like; but those are

not friendly or unfriendly foreigners, they are British subjects. Nothing has been alleged to their detriment, no charges have sheen made against them, and why should they be disfranchised and why should these impediments be placed in their way? I really cannot see the purpose of it. On the 24th May, 1918, we were just as wise as we are now. We had no greater reason on that date to be influenced by war difficulties than we are to-day-in fact, we were closer then to war conditions, and those conditions were more closely affecting us than they are at the present time. Nevertheless by an Act passed at that time, Chapter 20 of the Statutes of 1918, we said:
1. (1) Every female person shall be entitled to vote at a Dominion election who,-
(a)	is a British subject;
(b)	is of the full age of twenty-one years and upwardsand so on. lI could very well stop there, Mr. Chairman, and say that on the 24th day of May, 1918, we solemnly reached the conclusion that any woman in this country who was a British subject was entitled to vote. We had gone so far in that Act as not only to make them British subjects-those who were British subjects before-but to confer the franchise upon them. The hon. member for West Vancouver said a few minutes ago that we were not taking anything from these women which they now possess, and the House seemed to concur in the statement. But that cannot be the case, because by the Act from which I have quoted we conferred the right of voting on these very women from whom we are now taking it. Therefore we are depriving them of something which they now possess, a thing which we should not do. Now the Act from which I have quoted goes on to state as to the qualifications which a woman should possess to be entitled to vote:
(c)	possesses the qualifications which would entitle a male person to vote at a Dominion election in the province in which said female person seeks to vote: Provided that a married woman or an unmarried daughter living with her father or mother shall be deemed to have any necessary qualification as to property or income if the husband or either of the parents is so qualified.
We propose to repeal that Act by the Bill now before the House, and I think it is a serious matter for a deliberative body such as ours to coolly and deliberately say that	we were	wrong in	1918	whenwe conferred this right upon these women,	and that	we are	now	goingto take	it away	from them.	Therecertainly	ought to	be some	grave rea-

son before we do anything of that kind. If women should come to this country- French women, Italian women, Syrian women, Polish women-if any of these foreigners should come here, settle down, help to develop the country, and live happily and faithfully with their husbands bringing up their families, what reason is there for depriving these people of the right we conferred upon them a little over a year ago. I cannot see the reason of the justice of it, and I 'would be sorry that we should do anything so harsh and drastic in this Parliament unless we were moved to do so by the very best of reasons.
The hon. member for Dorchester this afternoon presented the legal nature of this question in a manner so perfectly clear that there seems to be no necessity of dealing further with that phase of it. .Section eleven of chapter 28 of the statutes of 1919 states:
The wife of a British subject shall be deemed to be a British subject, and the wife of an alien shall be deemed to be an alien.
There is a contradiction here. We say in one breath that this woman is a British subject, but in section 29 of the Bill that is now before us we say that it was impossible for her ever to be so. I ask the committee to consider the language of subsection 2 of section 29 of the Bill that is now before the committee:
For the purposes of this Act, the allegiance or nationality of a person, as it was at the birth of such person, shall be deemed Incapable of being changed-
We say there that it was absolutely impossible for the woman, or the children who are affected by this legislation to be what we say they are under the provisions of the Act we passed last year. As I said before, I submit that only very grave reasons indeed should cause us to put ourselves in such a position. I can understand this Parliament passing drastic legislation during the war, but now that we have signed Treaties of Peace with our leading enemies, why should we attempt to perpetuate the war spirit for the rest of our lives and inflict these disabilities on people who were friendly to us during the war? The hon. minister says that we can get over these difficulties by obtaining the certificate mentioned in this subsection. Ajs a rule when a judge is called upon to grant a certificate, certain things are laid down which must 'be proved before the certificate can be granted. I must confess that were I acting as a judge I would be entirely at a loss to know what kind of

evidence it was necessary to present to me to qualify an applicant for a certificate. If the minister is determined to force this thing through, I -would suggest that he add a clause stating specifically what a lawyer appearing for an applicant for one of these certificates would have to prove, so that he would know how to proceed before a judge. As the clause stands, everything is left absolutely to the discretion of the judge, and no lawyer can tell upon what grounds a judge will exercise that discretion. I submit further to the hon. minister, that in a district of probably 100 miles in length and 50 -miles in width with only a single judge there will be no accommodation to meet the requirements of the thousands of men and women who will have to apply for these certificates. When our men had to make application for exemption from military service we had a military tribunal at every turn of the road.

As we have the privilege of referring to some matters that came up before, I wish to make a few remarks regarding the item of $2,000,000 to provide for the construction of an icebreaking steamer to be used on the river -St. Lawrence. When this matter was under consideration before, some remarks were made to the effect that this icebreaker might be so constructed as to be used, on occasion, as an auxiliary to the Prince Edward Island car ferry plying between Port Borden and Cape Tormentine. I am particularly desirous that no improper impression may be made regarding this icebreaker. I-f I understand this item aright, the appropriation asked for is for the construction of a large icebreaker to ply on the river St. Lawrence to facilitate shipping -by keeping the river open in the winter season, and also for the purpose of assisting ships that may be in distress, and things of that sort. Should she be equipped with rails on her deck so as to be able to carry cars across the Strait as is done by the Prince Edward Island': car ferry, and so be able to assist that car-ferry if necessary, I shall be extremely-pleased; but there is nothing in the item to indicate that such is the case.
