If I am not properly informed and do not properly apprehend the meaning and intention of this appropriation, I shall be pleased if the minister will put me right,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The icebreaker will be used primarily for, the breaking of ice' in the St. Lawrence at the end of the season and towards the opening of navigation.

It will also keep the ice bridge open at Cap Rouge. It will be so powerful that it will be able to go to the assistance of ocean vessels leaving Montreal or Quebec late in the season. Last year, as the hon. member says, two of the Government steamers got stuck in the ice, and if we had had an icebreaker, there would have been no difficulty whatever in at once rescuing both these steamers from the ice pack in which they found themselves.
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) the otheT evening asked if I would look into the question of having the icebreaker so constructed that it would also serve as a car ferry. I do not know whether that is possible or not, but as I promised my hon. friend, the other evening, I shall take technical advice on the point when tenders are being called for. I cannot make any more definite statement at the moment. I know that all hon. members realize the importance to navigation on the St. Lawrence and on our east coast of having an icebreaker of this great strength. We only have two icebreakers at the present time, the Montcalm and the Lady Grey, neither of which is strong enough to cope with thick ice at certain seasons of the year. During the war an icebreaker similar to the one we are going to have constructed was sold to the Russian Government. The Earl Grey and the Minto were also sold, leaving us with only the Montcalm and the Lady Grey.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Inasmuch as I made the suggestion the other evening to which the minister has been kind enough to refer, I should like to say just a further word in regard to it. As the minister is aware, there is at the present time simply one car ferry between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Since that car ferry has come into use the people of the Island have become dependent on it to a degree that is almost exclusive. The result is that if anything should happen to the ferry at any moment, the Island will be shut off and there will not be available the variety of smaller craft that there would have been before people had come to rely so much on this car ferry. It is generally felt on the Island that there ought to be two car ferries, because if anything happens to the present one the people will be left without the accommodation to which they have become accustomed, and at certain seasons of the year that might prove very embarrassing indeed. It was for that reason I asked the minister to consider, at the time this great

icebreaker is being constructed, whether it would not be possible to have it so designed that in off seasons and in times of emergency it might be used to accomodate the people of the Island, just as a second car ferry would accommodate them if it existed. I would not have made the suggestion if it had not been that one or two marine experts have themselves expressed their opinion to me that this large icebreaker could be constructed in that way. It is perfectly true that its main purpose wdll he to break ice in the St. Lawrence, but I would point out to the minister that it will only be doing icebreaking work during the winter season. In the summer it will be lying idle, and it could then very well be used, I should think, as a car ferry while the present car ferry is laid up for a month or a couple of weeks for repairs, as it always is during the summer months. If this icebreaker were constructed in the way I have suggested it would not only serve that purpose but would also be available in time of emergency. What is wanted by the people of the Island, and those who are being served by the people of the Island is a two-car-ferry service, and just as soon as the Government feel justified in making this provision I think that such a service should be commenced. But in these days of much needed economy, if anything can be done, in the interval to fill in, if we can find a way to " kill two birds with one stone," I believe it will he very much in the interests of all concerned.

The ice in the St. Lawrence attains such a thickness that I am very doubtful if any icebreaker can be constructed that will be able to break the ice during the entire winter season. There is no question, however, that an icebreaker would be of very great service in the St. Lawrence during part of the season, and perhaps that is sufficient reason for the minister going ahead and getting built the most powerful icebreaker that can be constructed.
My object in rising, however, was not to discuss icebreaking on the 8t. Lawrence so much as the ice conditions on the Atlantic coast during the winter months. We endeavour to do a good deal of business from Sydney to Yarmouth and right up to the Bay of Fundy all the year round, but we are sometimes handicapped during the months of December, January and February by the ice conditions encountered on that coast. During the past two or three years

we have endeavoured to get the Department of Marine or the Department of Naval Affairs to help us out when ice conditions were such that we could not get along without help, and the department have always been willing to give us any assistance they could. But I have one complaint to make, and it is this: During the present season practically the only ice steamer which the department owns was tied up at the dock at Dartmouth from November till April. I refer to the Stanley, and I say it was bad business on the part of somebody to so arrange for the repairs to that steamer that she was tied up at the dock during all that time. If the Montcalm or some other icebreaker had been available the department would have been quite justified in having the Stanley laid up for repairs. It is well known that the Nova Scotia and Atlantic coast is very dangerous in the winter season. Nearly every week some vessel will be sending in S.O.S. calls for assistance from Sable island or the Atlantic ocean. Whenever a call came last winter there was no steamer of the department to send out to vessels in distress. On one occasion this year when the steamer Powattan owned by the United States, was crossing the Atlantic with troops, she lost her propeller and for ten days was at the mercy of the waves. It was only by an act of Providence that the steamer did not founder, perhaps with all hands on board. The Government at last did send the Lady Laurier to her assistance, and this vessel under the captaincy of Captain Travis, did good work, in company with United States tug boats, in helping to get the vessel to port. But my complaint is that the Stanley should have been available during the winter months to go to the assistance of steamers in distress. The only steamer which the department could send to the assistance of vessels off the Nova Scotia coast was a little steamer called the Petrel, which is one of the fishery protective service boats. I may say that the captain and crew of that steamer did everything possible for the people at Shelburne, Lockport, Liverpool and Lunenburg, but the trouble was the steamer was not large enough to do the work that was required of her. If the Stanley or a steamer of that class had been available, and the Stanley should have been available, business men along the coast of Nova Scotia would not have had to suffer the inconvenience they did during those months. I am not finding fault, so much as pointing out
to the minister that next year he should provide a steamer for this service so that business men along the coast of Nova Scotia need not be put to the inconvenience they were this winter. I understand the Department of Naval Affairs has a steamer called the Acadia which could have done this work, but she was laid up at Halifax. I would suggest that next year the steamer be stationed at Lunenburg or Liverpool to serve the people along the coast of Nova Scotia.

I do not yet know who that gentleman is, nor do I care; but I want to say that the Government should not come here and tell us that the appointments are made by the Civil Service Commission, and then go outside and make them through the Commissioner of Customs or anybody else. I have no objection from a personal standpoint to this appointment and it might be quite proper for the Commissioner of Customs or the Minister of Customs to make the appointment-although I think the Commissioner of Customs is the "goat" in this case because the Acting Minister of Customs was the gentleman who actually exercised the power and not the commissioner. I do find fault, however, upon the ground that the Minister of Marine, in my opinion, is just as capable as the Minister of Customs and should have the selection of his own officers. When I found this gentleman had been appointed Acting Registrar of Shipping I first took the matter up with the Customs Department, but could get no satisfaction there. I then applied to the Civil Service Commission, and I have a letter from the chairman of that body in which he definitely states that the Civil Service Commission had nothing whatever to do with this appointment. I then wrote the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), who at that time was Acting Minister of Marine, and he expressed considerable surprise that the appointment had gone through without consultation with him, either as the Acting Minister of Marine or as the godfather of the Civil Service Commission. When the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) himself returned to his office last winter I wrote him a letter and asked him how and why the appointment was made, and received a letter from him to the following effect:
Office of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of Canada,
Ottawa, 31st December, 1919.
Dear Sir,-In answer to your letter of the 18th instant, I beg to inform you that the practice which has obtained in Canada since Confederation has been that the collector, or other chief officer of Customs, at a port of registry is ex officio the Registrar of Shipping, and the Canadian Order in Council passed on the 26th March, 1874, instituting Lunenburg a port of registry, appointed the collector of Customs at the port Registrar of Shipping.
... , . .. - - [DOT]

When Mr. Mack, therefore, was appointed acting collector of Customs at Lunenburg, he ipso facto became acting registrar of shipping. X am not, as you may well understand, familiar with the manner in which Mr. Mack and Mr. Anderson were appointed to the Customs Service.
I gather from your letter that no permanent appointment as collector has yet been made. Following the previous custom and the requirement of the Order in Council creating Lunenburg a port of registry whoever becomes the permanent officer will be the registrar.
Yours very truly,
C. C. Ballantyne.
You will see, Mr. Chairman, that neither the Minister of Marine nor his officials had anything whatever to do with the appointment of this official. Yet if there is one port in Nova Scotia where the office of registrar is an important one it is the port of Lunenburg, not because the business is so large but because there are so many transactions. The business done is on a co-operative basis there being sometimes as many as sixty-four owners in one ship. I do not think any such condition exists in any other port of Canada as exists there, and for that reason there are more transfers of ships or shares in ships by the registrar at Lunenburg than perhaps anywhere else in the world. The appointment of the officer in question was a very important one, and it seems to me that the Minister of Marine should certainly have had something to do with it. For this reason:	If
the Registrar of shipping does not act in conformity with the law, the Minister of Marine or his officials here will get the blame. Therefore that minister should not for one moment longer allow the Minister of Customs, or any officer belonging to the Customs Department, to make such an appointment. It is time the Order in Council passed in 1874 was repealed, and the Minister of Marine given the power to select his own officials. I repeat that the office of registrar in the town of Lunenburg is an important one, and if the present incumbent is only acting registrar, the Minister of Marine should be very careful before he allows the Minister of Customs to make that appointment permanent.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Possibly the hon. gentleman is aware that the Minister of Marine has not the authority, under the Shipping Act, to appoint registrars of shipping. That power is vested in the Minister of Customs only.
That is what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The passage of an
Order in Council would not be sufficient
to meet the situation. I would have to bring in legislation repealing clause 11 of the Shipping Act which vests the authority in the Minister of Customs.

The minister did not grasp the purport of what I said. Perhaps I did not -make myself sufficiently clear. I did not say the minister could Temedy matters by passing an Order in Council. I said [DOT]that the minister was acting at the present time under an Order in Council which was passed in 1874. I further said that it was high time that that Order in Council was repealed, and that it was a shame that the minister at present did not have the power to appoint his own officials.

I understand
that at present the registrar of shipping charges fees, and that the owner of a ship has to pay all the expenses of a survey and of registry. Is this money spent at the head office or is it expended in the several ports?

speechtext: The money is spent at the head office. Owing to the large increase of Canadian registered tonnage there are far more ships being registered now than has ever been the case in past yeaTS. Is any portion of this
money applied to augmenting the salary of the collector of customs-is that the way it is done, or does the collector of customs receive an extra salary for these duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The various registrars throughout Canada are paid by a scale of fees as follows: For vessels under fifty tons net register, $3-
That is the fee which a shipowner pays?

While the minister is getting that information will he permit me to say that the owners of the vessel pay all the fees in connection with the registry of vessels when they are built. Is it also a fact that the vessel owners when they transfer the ships or shares pay $1 for getting a bill of sale and fifty cents for a declaration of ownership. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I find that I confused the fees for surveys with the registry

of shipping. There are no fees charged for the registry of a ship.
The owner pays the cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Agencies, rents and contingencies-5198,000.

I would like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter concerning the agency at Halifax. Air. Harvey, who is in charge of that agency, is, so far as I am aware, a capable official. For a great many years the Department of Marine and Naval Affairs has been paying for a telephone in his house, and this telephone was a very great convenience to the business men of Halifax or of any other part of Nova Scotia when there is any trouble along the shore and they wish to communicate with Mr. Harvey. But I notice that that "great family journal," the Halifax Herald-the minister will know what paper I am referring to-publishes a cartoon headed, "Cutting the life-line." I do not know if the minister can see this cartoon which I am holding up for his attention, but it refers to the fact that the Marine Department has ordered Mr. Harvey to discontinue his house telephone or they would hold him responsible for the expense. It is as important to have a telephone in Mr. Harvey's house as in his office for the purpose of looking after the work on the Nova Scotia coast, and I feel sure the Halifax Herald was mistaken when it circulated that report all over the province to the worry of a number of our business men who appreciate the importance of being able to keep in touch with Mr. Harvey in case of emergency. I would like to know if this statement is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member is quite correct when he surmises that the article is unwarranted. The telephone is not going to be taken out of Mr, Harvey's house.
Salaries and allowances to lightkeepers- $650,000.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the salaries of the lightkeepers. When the items for bonuses were before the House I called to his attention the inadequate salaries paid to these men, and I was told that the bonus regulations did not apply to them. I find from the Auditor General's report that the salaries range from $84 to about $300. These salaries were small enough when the cost of living was normal, when, for instance, a barrel of flour could be purchased for $3 or $4, as against the current price of $14

or $15,-and so with other commodities. On a former occasion I urged the necessity of helping these men, and I hope that the minister will now see his way clear to give their case his favourable consideration, for these men perform splendid service at various isolated places on the coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Will these lighthouse keepers share in the bonus we voted the other day for the Civil Service? I put that question to the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), and I received a very nice smile from him, but no answer. So I expect the smile was affirmative, and that these men will share in the bonus.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The $60,000 voted at the two previous sessions represented bonuses to these men, but there will be no further bonuses granted from the vote my hon. friend refers to. (Mr. Leger) a new classification has been made by the Civil Service Commission, and all grades of lighthouse keepers will now receive higher salaries.
Air. GA'UVREAU: If I am well informed, a delegation from the lighthouse keepers came here some time ago, and they left entirely pleased with what they were told, fully expecting that what they asked for would be granted to them. While I am on my (feet I would call the attention of the minister to a request for a cable between Green Island and the mainland in the County of Temiscouata. I am sorry to say that, according to a letter I received from the department, no record is kept of the understanding arrived at many years ago between the Hon. Mr. Brodeur and myself. It was understood at that time that connection would be made between Red island in

the St. Lawrence and Green island lighthouse and then with the mainland by means of the Kamouraska Telephone Company. The understanding was that the Government would provide the cable and the company would pay all expenses for laying the cable and the cost of operation. It was found at that time that that was too much for 'the company. The company now ask me if there is any way of getting 8,000 feet of cable to connect Green island with the mainland. Everybody who knows the river Sf. Lawrence opposite the river Saguenay realizes the difficulties that exist in that part of the river. It is one of the most dangerous spots on the river St. Lawrence, and if the department can afford the expense of providing a cable to connect Green Island lighthouse with the mainland, a great deal of expense will be saved to the department, and vessels going up or down the St. Lawrence will be afforded greater safety. I was told the other day by the deputy minister-and I think he is right- that it would be hard at the present time ito ask for an appropriation for 8,000 feet of cable; but in view of the fact that if 8,000 feet of cable could be provided to connect Green Island lighthouse with the mainland, great aid will be given to navigation on the river St. Lawrence, I hope the minister, who received so well the deputation of lighthouse keepers, will see his way clear to grant that request. It is only for 8,000 feet of cable, and the company will lay the cable and pay all the cost of operation in the years to come. The amount is a small one after all, and the minister would be wise in granting that request, thereby ensuring greater safety to vessels plying on the river St. Lawrence.
What does the -hon. member mean by Green island? Does he -mean lie Verte?

Green island is an
island in the centre of the St. Lawrence and lie Verte is the parish on the north side.
Mr. BUREAiU: Is it called Green Island or lie Verte?

On the map it is
called Green island, but we can say either Green island or He Verte. I think the minister will understand me, all right. I would not like him to think I came from a "green" part of the country.

No, the hon. member is all right. I am asking this question merely for the purpose of information because I
know that island is designated in our local statutes as lie Verte. I know that a Geographical Commission was appointed to rebaptize certain localities, but I had occasion to look up some matters in connection with this island, and in the local statues I found it is designated as lie Verte. Mr. B'ALLANTYNE: I have not as perfect a knowledge of both languages as my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) has, but I do not see any difference between He Verte and Green -Island. This is not a question
of knowledge, and I do not want the minister to think I am trying to read him a lesson in either French or English. That has never been my custom and I am not going to start now, but I want to know how the name "Green Island" occurred on the map when the property is designated in -our statutes as lie Verte. If the change has been made by the Geographical Cbm-*mission, well and good; but as this may lead to confusion, I want to find out whether Green island is the same piece of land, as is designated in our statutes as He Verte.

What about my cable now?
iMr. BALLANTYNE-: In reply to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau), I am. informed that no record can be found on the files of the Marine Department that my predecessor, the Hon. Mr. Brodeur, made any such arrangement. I cannot make a definite promise to the hon. member to-night. I have already informed the members of -the committee that we must practise economy, -but I shall be glad to look into the matter, and if there is any possible way of .meeting the views of the hon. member, it will be a pleasure for me to do so.
Mr. MoISAAC: I am not sure whether or not I understood the minister aright regarding the increase of $50,000 in the whole appropriation for salaries and allowances to lighthouse keepers, whether it is for the purpose of increasing the salaries or whether it is to be applied by way of bonus. I understand that for the past two or three years certain of the lighthouse keepers-I do not know about them all-have received a bonus. Is 'this all the increase, or will any of those lighthouse

keepers participate by way of bonus in the proposed appropriation of $12,500,000 for bonuses to civil servants?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They will not participate in the bonus, part of which has already 'been voted. A moment ago I referred to the fact that at the last session of Parliament, and the previous one, $60,000 had been voted on each occasion. The Civil Service Commission have gone over the salaries of the lighthouse keepers; I have the reclassification here, and if 1 passes the House, there will be a substantial increase in salaries for all of the lg 1 house keepers. If 'the hon. member wishes me to let him know what the increase will be for any particular class of lighthouse keepers, I shall be very glad to give him the information.

I think every member of the committee will agree with me that if there are any public officials in Canada who deserve to be well paid for their services, they are the men who look after the lighthouses on both coasts and on the St. Lawrence and other rivers. Most of these men have to live on islands away from their friends and relatives; they deserve every consideration on the part of this Government, and I feel sure that the minister had that in mind in increasing the appropriation by the reasonable amount of $50,000.
I rose particularly to refer to the item for maintenance and repairs to Dominion steamers and icebreakers, which item was discussed in my absence. I should like to refer for a moment to the salaries or wages paid to the crews of Government steamers. The men on our Government steamers, many of whom I know very well, are the poorest paid men in Canada. Let me take, for instance, the Government steamer "Lady Laurier," which has done excellent work on the Nova Scotia coast. I find, looking at the Auditor General's report, that Captain Travis, captain of this vessel, received last year only $1,600, or in round figures about $135 a month. That is disgraceful. No captain of a small hundred-ton boat receives a smaller wage than Captain Travis of the "Lady Laurier," and a man with his experience and ability should receive at least $200 a month. I do not know Captain Travis personally, except to meet him perhaps once in two years, but it is a shame that a man of his experience should be receiving only $1,600 a year and $100 of a bonus from the people of this country for his services. On the same page, I find that the first officer of that boat received only $100 per month.

A mate on either a small steamer or a sailing vessel receives $150 a month, and it seems to me that a mate on a Government steamer (should receive a larger salary than a mate on a small ship.
I would suggest to the minister that he go over the salary schedule of his officers and",, see if something cannot be done towards compensating adequately these hardworking men. They have to go along the coast of Nova Scotia and out in mid-Atlantic in all kinds of weather. In the summer they encounter fog, and in the winter cold weather and storms, and it seems to me they are certainly deserving of an increase. One thing I cannot understand is why they stay in the Government service for such a small salary. Any time during the last five years it would have been no trouble for Captain Travis to get $200 or $250 a month. The same thing applies to the captain of the icebreaker Montcalm, Captain Hearn, who is one of the most capable navigators in Canada. There is no question that he is a first-class man, yet he only receives $135 a month. Why, any ordinary nigger gets almost that much on board a ship. I might say that on little fishing schooners cooks are receiving $250 a month. Captain Hearn's cook gets only $80 a month. That is a scandalous state of affairs. The same is true of the steamer Stanley. The Stanley is an absolute necessity on 'the coast. Her captain is very much underpaid. Captain Slawenwhite, the mate, has lived in Halifax for ten or fifteen years. He has no vote in my county, he votes in Halifax, so it cannot be said I am trying to catch a vote or talking for political purposes. He .possesses a master's certificate and is paid only $110 or $120 per month. When he was at sea before he got into the King's uniform, and when wages were much lower, he was receiving perhaps $150 in wages alone, and if he left the Government service he would get at least $200 a month. I bring these matters to the attention of the minister because I have received several communications from men on the Government steamers within the last few months asking me to point out to the minister and to the committee when the Estimates were up how inadequate their salaries were. The minister should certainly do something to give these men a decent wage, for they cannot live on the wages they get. Captain Slawenwhite lives in Halifax, and I do not see how he can live there and raise his family on $110 a month. I appeal once more to the minister to see if something cannot be done to pay these men a decent wage.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
has been quoting the salaries. The blue-book does not show the bonuses.
I mentioned bonuses.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Hearn of Ihe Montcalm gets $140 a month and a bonus of $19. The captain of the Stanley gets $135 a month and $17 bonus. Fishing vessels.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am glad to know there is so much money in the fishing business "that they can afford to pay a cook $250 a month.
The crew pay half and the owners half.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They must have first-class chefs on those vessels. While I am in sympathy with doing everything that can be done to pay as good salaries as possible to the crews of the Government ships, I would certainly not be prepared to recommend to the committee a salary of $250 a month for cooks. We have very good cooks on our ships, and we get them for very much less than that. We pay the chief cook $70 a month, and the second cook $45 a month. There is a great deal of difference between $70 and $200 a month. Under re-classification all the members of the crews of the Government ships will have an increase in salary, but we cannot hope to compete with the very fanciful salaries paid by fishing vessels.

This $250 is only paid by
fishing vessels with a crew perhaps of nineteen men. A vessel with a crew of perhaps six or seven men would pay their cooks $100 a month. If the owners of sailing vessels in Nova Scotia can afford to pay their cooks $100, surely the people of Canada will be willing to pay their cooks an equal amount, if not a little more.
Tbe minister has referred to the reclassification of the Civil Service. I would not advise him to pay his officers according to the re-classification schedules. If I were minister, I would kick up my heels if anybody asked me to go by that classification. It provides for able seamen, for instance, a salary of only $60 a month. The minister must know that it is impossible in this enlightened' age to get able seamen for that amount. While the Arthur Young
Company might be able to get them, nobody on the Atlantic or Pacific coast could hire his sailors for $60, and if the minister had to hold his ships in port until he got them at that price they would be tied up much longer than they are at present. Under the re-classification, a first-class master is to get $160 a month, a seoond-class master $140, third-class $120, and fourth-class $105. A first-class mate is supposed to get $100, and a second-class mate $80 a month. The minister ought not to be willing to pay the rates set out in this classification, or to -continue to pay the wages he is now paying to the men on these steamers. These men should be paid for doing Government work just as much as they would be paid by any private corporation.

I notice an increase of $50,000 in the item for salaries for lighthouse keepers. I -should like to know if this increase applies generally -to lighthouse keepers and whether they will all participate in the increase. I understand there is to be a classification. Will every class of lighthouse keeper participate in some degree in the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The increase of
$50,000 applies only to certain classes, only to the more important lighthouses, not lighthouses in -minor waters. It applies to lighthouses -that are Tunning all the year Toun-d.

I understand that the keepers in the smaller lighthouses were poorly paid, and I hardly think that it was a proper adjustment to spend the -money altogether on the larger lighthouses while the smaller ones do not participate.

Does this increase apply
only to Nova Scotia? Are we on lake Erie and lake Ontario to expect an increase for lighthouse keepers as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The classification of the Civil Service applies to all lighthouse keepers throughout Canada. In answer to my hon. friend (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) I may say that the minor lighthouse keepers give only a portion of their time to looking after lights. I admit that their remuneration is small, -but their duties are not very onerous. However, they also will come in for an increase under the re-classification.

I suppose it is
true that the lighthouse keepers on the St. Lawrence and -the Great Lakes, which are frozen up part of the year, have considerable spare time during which they can add

to their income. But that is not true as regards the Maritime Provinces and the coasts where the lighthouse keepers work all winter, night and day. They have always to be on hand to light the lamps, and some of these men are poorly paid indeed. In the increase of $50,000 I trust they will participate.

I desire to add a word or two on behalf of the small lighthouse keepers. It may be true that those on the inland waters where the lakes and rivers are frozen part of the year have that portion of the winter months to themselves to do something else, but I should like to know what there is for them to do during that time. There is very little opportunity for them to make any money during the winter months, and practically speaking they have to depend entirely on the salaries they get for that work. I can see no reason why men occupying these important and responsible positions should be treated any differently, so far as bonuses are concerned, from any other men in the Civil Service. Where men who occupy clerical positions in the departments in Ottawa and perform their duties faithfully and well, receive salaries on which it is considered they cannot live, we unanimously agree that it is right that they should share in the bonus. Why, therefore, should the bonus not be given to those men who are tied down to such responsible duties as these men have to perform? In a city like Ottawa civil servants are in a position to combine their forces and press their demands in a way in which those who occupy isolated government positions cannot; but that does not strengthen the claim of the urban civil servants, nor does it weaken the claim of those who are not fortunate enough to be able to join forces and urge their case upon the Government. It is merely a question of fair play and just treatment, and I want to place myself on record as being of the opinion that if the bonus can be justifiably paid to civil servants in Ottawa and elsewhere it can just as reasonably and justifiably be extended so as to supplement the very small salaries which these lightkeepers have hitherto received.

I am not quite clear as to the division line between the large and the small lighthouses. Perhaps the minister can tell us what class of lighthouse peepers will get the increase.
. Mr. BALLANTYNE: There are nineteen classes in all. The bonuses voted for the past two sessions of $60,000 each were dis-

They of course would not share in this additional *$50,000, but all the lighthouse keepers in ,the Maritime Provinces and on the Great Lakes will. Those men who hang up lights would not participate in the increase.

As a matter of
fact they are not lighthouse keepers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, but we have no .other name for them.

speechtext:
The question which the hon. gentleman 'asks is a poser. For ,the time being, I regret to say, I cannot answer it. I shall look up the information, ,and in the meantime, in order that we may make some progress, I would ask, with the consent of the hon. member, that we propeed to the next item.
Maintenance and repairs to lighthouses- $750,000.

I have endeavoured to .keep in touch with the matter up to now but I have not received very much information or encouragement. May I ask what has been done in connection with the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am afraid I have [DOT]to tell the same old story. Owing to the expenses of the war, the large public debt, *and the necessity for rigid economy, [DOT]the matter will have to stand in abeyance [DOT]as a great many other important items have had to stand. But as soon as I can get a sufficient vote I shall be glad to see that it [DOT]is attended to.

I am just as anxious as the minister that we should practise all the economy possible, but I am afraid that things have come to such a pass in the department that their economies are rather destructive than constructive. The port is

a new one; a lot of shipping goes on there,-and there is one light. What we want is ; 9 range light which will enable our vessels I to come at night, because the coast in thaty vicinity is very rough. If any of our flshingH vessels were wrecked on the coast, it would f* he remembered that the minister and those!-associated with him had destroyed the only; means of safety we have, that is, our life-' saving station at Chetieamp, in this fever for economy in small matters, while most-extravagant in large matters. I for one cannot see where the economy comes in when the lives and property of the fishermen are at stake. But, so far as this small item is concerned, I wish to put myself on record as not- accepting the argument of the minister based on the ground of economy.
